div.p: Understanding the end-to-end temporal behavior of distributed systems is a fundamental concern in real-time computing. Meeting timing requirements is critical to many computer applications. These real-time systems employ a schedulability test to determine whether each task can meet its deadline. In this paper, we extend Liu and Abdelzaher's work by introducing laxity as the priority of the real-time tasks. A Least-Laxity-First (LLF) scheduling algorithm assigns higher priority to a task with the least laxity, and has been proven to be optimal for uniprocessor systems. We compare this laxity based scheduling policy with deadline monotonic scheduling (DMS), shortest-job-first scheduling (SJF), and velocity monotonic scheduling (VMS). Simulations show that the proposed laxity-based scheduling policy is a feasible approach for real-time admission control.

div.head: S
div.p: ince the seminal work of Liu and Layland [1], where they derived the well-known 69% utilization bound for rate monotonic scheduling (RMS) on a single processor system, many real-time scheduling algorithms have been proposed in the literature. Bini and Buttazzo [2] extended the utilization bounds to multiprocessor real-time systems, and they considered resource constraints and presented a single stage utilization bound that was less pessimistic than Liu and Layland's work. Kuo and Mok [3] improved the Liu and Layland's bound by collapsing harmonic tasks into one chain. They proved that the bound is a function of the number of the harmonic chains and not the number of individual tasks. This bound was further improved by considering information specific to the task set such as the actual values of task periods [4]. Park et al. [5] refined this approach by introducing a design-time technique for computing bounds. Wu et al. [6] proposed a framework for deriving feasible regions for arbitrary real-time systems based on network calculus. They used the notion of workload rate to measure the resource demand within a period of time that is proportional to the deadline of the task. Abdelzaher and Lu [7] described a constant time utilization based schedulability test for aperiodic tasks on a uniprocessor for fixed-priority scheduling. Andersson and Ekelin [8] proposed an exact admission controller algorithm for earliest-deadline-first (EDF) systems subjected to aperiodic tasks. Liu and Abdelzaher [9] derived a general expression for a non-utilization-based schedulability bound. The bound applies to a generalized abstract load metric that is defmed for a given system as a function of its particular scheduling policy.

Recently, aperiodic tasks were considered as an exception to periodic task systems, and they could be converted into periodic tasks. For example, this includes the slack server [10], the sporadic server [11], and the deferrable server [12]. Han and Park [13] studied the predictability of least laxity first (LLF) scheduling algorithm on multiprocessor real-time systems. Oh and Yang [14] proposed a modified least-Iaxity first scheduling algorithm for real-time tasks. More papers on real-time scheduling include [15]- [19].

We briefly give some explanations about the OMS, SJF and VMS scheduling policies here. In OMS, tasks are assigned priorities according to their deadlines; the task with the shortest deadline being assigned the highest priority. Deadline-monotonic priority assignment is a priority assignment policy used with fixed priority pre-emptive scheduling. In SJF, a scheduling policy selects the waiting process with the smallest execution time to execute next. SJF is advantageous because of its simplicity and because it maximizes process throughput (in terms of the number of processes run to completion in a given amount of time). It also minimizes the average amount of time each process has to wait until its execution is complete. In VMS, priorities are set proportionally to the ratio of the end-to-end deadline to the number of stages to be traversed. Priority is higher when the deadline lower and when the number of stages to be traversed is more. If two tasks have the same end-to-end deadline but a different number of stages to traverse, the one with more stages should be given a higher priority.

In this paper, we propose a new fixed-priority scheduling policy by using laxity values as its priority. This is based on Liu and Abdelzaher's previous work [9] where they derived non-utilization bounds for arbitrary fixed-priority policies. We compare this laxity-based scheduling policy with deadline monotonic scheduling (OMS), shortest-job-first scheduling (SJF), and velocity monotonic scheduling (VMS). Simulation results confirm that the proposed method in this paper is a feasible approach for fixed-priority real time admission control.
Submission date: January 16, 2011.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II gives a short introduction about Liu and Abdelzaher's method [9] for admission control, and proposes a new scheduling policy for real-time admission control by using the laxity value as the priority of a task. Section III conducts some experiments in order to show that the proposed method is a feasible choice for real time admission control. Finally, Section IV draws the conclusions of the paper and gives future work to be done.

In this paper, we introduce least-laxity-first (LLF) real time scheduling for fixed priority tasks. LLF is a scheduling algorithm that assigns priority based on the laxity time of a process. Laxity time is the amount of time left after ajob has started.

Its most common use is in real-time systems, especially those with multiple processors. It imposes the simple constraint that each process on each available processor possesses the same run-time. This makes it a suitable choice for real-time systems.

The LLF scheduling is most useful in systems comprising mainly aperiodic tasks, because no prior assumptions are made on the events' rate of occurrence. This scheduling policy can be used for processor utilization up to 100%. LLF is a little more general than EDF for multiprocessors because it takes into account laxity time, which is more meaningful than deadline for tasks of mixed computing sizes. In addition, LLF offers probably more graceful degradations.

div.head: III. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: In this section, we conducted some experiments in order to simulate the feasibility of the proposed scheduling policy for fixed-priority tasks. We assume that the computation time of different stages is independent, and end-to-end deadlines are selected uniformly from a range. The arrival process is Poisson. Scheduling at each stage is based on a priority which is monotonically decreasing with x. The priority is kept constant for all execution stages of the same task. We compared the LLF scheduling policy with three existing scheduling policies (OMS, SJF and VMS). To balance load among all machines, we can select the same mean computation times at all stages. The number of stages of a task is set to be N= 1 0, and the probability that a task selects a stage is p=0.5. The mean number of stages a task will use is N x p = 5. The average stage load is approximately equal. In addition, we let the stages be always traversed in the same order.

We have calculated the average stage-utilization for the proposed scheduling policy and three existing scheduling policies OMS, SJF, and VMS. The input workload is varied from 40% to 200% of a single stage capacity. This means that the sum of computation times of all tasks generated over the duration of the experiment is varied from 40% to 200% of the length of the experiment. Fig. 1 shows the curves of our proposed LLF scheduling policy, and OMS, SJF and VMS. It can be seen that LLF is not as good as OMS and VMS scheduling, but it is much better than SJF scheduling. OMS is the best scheduling policy in this experiment. This indicates that LLF scheduling is a feasible choice for real time admission control. We also multiply a constant K to the laxity priority Xi = Kxi for K =0.1, 1.0 and 10.0. Fig. 2 shows the curves of our proposed method for different values of K.

From the figure it can be seen that the constant K=1.0 is a good choice for our proposed method in this paper. In addition, the constant K = 1.0 is much better than K =0.1 in the figure. This indicates that multiplying a constant is not necessary for LLF-based real-time admission control.

div.head: IV. CONCLUSION
div.p: Utilization bounds for schedulability are one of the simplest approaches for admission control in real-time systems. Even though they are not resource optimal, they offer the advantages of simplicity and computational efficiency. Liu and Abdelzaher [9] proposed a universal bound that was customized to any fixed-priority scheduling policy by choosing the corresponding load metric. In this paper, we extend Liu and Abdelzaher's non-utilization bound to LLF scheduling. We have compared this scheduling policy with the OMS, SJF, and VMS scheduling policies. Simulation results demonstrate that this is a feasible method for real time admission control.

Future work will be done by deriving the non-utilization bounds for periodic tasks, where tighter bounds could be found. In addition, we may try to find the optimal function x in order to improve the derived bounds for real-time scheduling. It would also be interesting to study the scheduling policies for dynamic priority tasks.

We may investigate a combination of existing scheduling policies in order to find better scheduling policies. The new priority assignment can be used to achieve a more fair performance among tasks. For example, we can minimize the average response time, min L'i where Xi is the new allocated priority for task i. The reason why we divide Xi in the above equation is because we do not want the response time of lower priority tasks to degrade the overall system performance.
More research needs to be done in order to improve the existing real-time scheduling policies published in the literature.
